hints: Think of one familiar clothing fibre made by ester links and one made by amide links, for example Terylene or nylon.
walkthrough:
Sort polyesters from polyamides**
Remember the link tells you the family. If the polymer chain is joined by ester groups, $\text{-COO-}$, it is a polyester. If it is joined by amide groups, $\text{-CONH-}$, it is a polyamide. Both can be synthetic.

Pick well known examples**
For polyester, Terylene, also called PET or poly(ethylene terephthalate), is the classic clothes and bottles example. Polylactic acid is another accepted polyester. For polyamide, nylon is the classic fibre, while Kevlar and Nomex are aromatic polyamides.

Final answer: polyester: Terylene (PET) or polylactic acid (PLA)
polyamide: nylon or Kevlar or Nomex

hints: Recall what the word condensation means in polymer chemistry, joining two functional groups with loss of a small stable molecule.
walkthrough:
See why a small molecule must leave**
When a $\text{-OH}$ group and a $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group join to make an ester, or a $\text{-NH}_2$ group and a $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group join to make an amide, the $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-H}$ fragments combine. That is the signature of condensation, the chain grows and a small molecule is expelled.

Name the usual leaving molecule**
Most commonly that molecule is water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. If an acyl chloride is used instead of a carboxylic acid, the eliminated molecule is $\text{HCl}$.
Final answer: water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) or hydrogen chloride ($\text{HCl}$ / hydrochloric acid)

hints: Look inside each repeat unit for a hydrolysable link, an ester $\text{-COO-}$ or an amide $\text{-CONH-}$, versus an all carbon backbone.
Recall that condensation polymers can be hydrolysed by water, acids or enzymes, while polyalkenes with C-C chains cannot be easily broken down.
walkthrough:
Use the functional group as your detector**
Biodegradable in this syllabus essentially means hydrolysable in nature. Scan for $\text{C=O}$ joined to O or to N. Polymer A has $\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-COO-}$, an ester. Polymer B has $\text{-COO-}$ on both sides of the benzene ring, also an ester. Polymer D has $\text{-CONH-}$, an amide. All three can be attacked by water.

Spot the odd one out**
Polymer C looks completely different. Its backbone is $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)(CO}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)-}$, a substituted alkene polymer (Perspex type). There is an ester in the side chain, but the main chain is all strong C-C single bonds formed by addition polymerisation. That C-C backbone is not hydrolysed under natural conditions, so C is not biodegradable.

Assign the ticks**
So tick A, tick B, leave C blank, tick D. That gives A yes, B yes and C no, D yes for the two marks.

Final answer: A biodegradable (tick): polyester with ester link
B biodegradable (tick): polyester with ester link
C not biodegradable: addition polymer with hydrocarbon backbone only
D biodegradable (tick): polyamide with amide link

hints: Split polymer B at the two ester $\text{-COO-}$ links and add $\text{-OH}$ back to the carbonyl side and $\text{-H}$ back to the oxygen side.
Recall that a polyester from a diacid plus a diol gives one aromatic diacid fragment and one $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-OH}$ type fragment.
walkthrough:
Cut the ester links in your head**
Polymer B is $\text{-[CO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O]-}_n$. Imagine hydrolysing both $\text{CO-O}$ bonds. Each $\text{CO-O}$ becomes $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on the acid side and $\text{HO-}$ on the alcohol side.

Rebuild the two monomers**
The left hand fragment gives $\text{HO}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ with the two $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups para to each other at positions 1 and 4. The right hand fragment gives $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-OH}$, ethane-1,2-diol. Draw both with full $\text{-OH}$ groups, benzene ring with circle, and correct connectivity. This is the classic Terylene pair.

Final answer: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (ethane-1,2-diol) and $\text{1,4-HO}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, terephthalic acid). Accept the 1,4-diacyl chloride $\text{ClOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCl}$ or 1,4-diester equivalent.

hints: Compare the formulas and count how many basic $\text{-NH}_2$ groups versus acidic $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups each amino acid has.
walkthrough:
Count acids versus bases**
T is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$ and U is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$. Both have one $\text{-NH}_2$ and one $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. V is $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$, lysine type. It has two $\text{-NH}_2$ groups and only one $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$.

Link extra amine to higher pH**
Amine groups are basic because they accept $\text{H}^+$ to form $\text{-NH}_3^+$. With an extra $\text{-NH}_2$ on its side chain, V removes more $\text{H}^+$ from water and produces more $\text{OH}^-$, so its aqueous solution is the most basic with the highest pH.
Final answer: V has the highest pH because it has two amine / $\text{NH}_2$ groups (an extra amine on the side chain / R group) which can be protonated to give a basic solution.

hints: List the possible ordered pairs from T and U, remembering that T-U is different from U-T because the ends are different.
walkthrough:
Treat order as important**
A dipeptide has an N-terminus and a C-terminus, so swapping the order makes a new molecule. With two choices for position 1 (T or U) and two choices for position 2 (T or U), you get $2 \times 2 = 4$ combinations: T joined to T, T joined to U, U joined to T, and U joined to U.
Final answer: four different dipeptides: TT, TU, UT, UU

hints: Look past the hydrocarbon side chains and find the polar parts of the backbone, the $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ of each peptide link plus terminal $\text{-NH}_3^+$ and $\text{-CO}_2^-$ groups.
Recall which two types of strong attraction water can make with polar O and N atoms and with full charges.
walkthrough:
Find the hydrophilic spots**
It is true the R groups contain a lot of C and H, which alone would be hydrophobic. But every peptide bond $\text{-CONH-}$ has a highly polar $\text{C=O}$ oxygen with lone pairs and a polar $\text{N-H}$ hydrogen. The chain ends and some side chains also exist as $\text{-NH}_3^+$ and $\text{-CO}_2^-$ in water.

Bond those spots to water**
Water is excellent at hydrogen bonding. Its $\text{O-H}$ hydrogens bond to the carbonyl oxygens, and its oxygens bond to the amide $\text{N-H}$ hydrogens. Where there are full charges, water forms even stronger ion-dipole attractions with $\text{-NH}_3^+$ and $\text{-CO}_2^-$. These attractions release enough energy to overcome water-water bonds, so many polypeptides dissolve despite their carbon content.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonds form between water and the O / N atoms (C=O and N-H groups) of the polypeptide backbone and polar side chains.
Ion-dipole attractions form between water and $\text{NH}_3^+$ / $\text{CO}_2^-$ terminal or side chain groups.
